read.sections.0.text.back: No one alive today has ever seen the world as it was 1,000 years ago, so how do we know about it? Historians are people who study the past by looking for sources. A source is anything at all that gives us information about the past. Letters, photos, paintings, tools, receipts, buildings and maps can be sources, and so can memories shared by older people. Each source is like a clue in a puzzle. The Riverstone painting, receipt and diary are three sources about one market. Historians use clues like these as evidence, then make claims about what happened.
read.sections.0.text.source: Nobody alive today saw the world as it was 1,000 years ago, so how do we know about it? A historian is a person who studies the past by looking for sources. A source is anything that gives us information about the past. Letters, photographs, drawings, tools, receipts, buildings and maps can all be sources, and so can memories that older people share. Each source is like a clue in a puzzle. The Riverstone drawing, receipt and diary are three sources about one market. A historian uses clues like these as evidence and then makes a claim about what happened.

read.sections.0.simpler.back: No one today saw the world in olden times. So, how do we learn about it? Historians are people who study the past. Historians look at sources. Sources tell us something about the past. A source can be a letter, a photo or a tool. A source can also be a story from an older person. Each source is a clue. We use clues as evidence. Evidence helps us make claims about the past.
read.sections.0.simpler.source: Nobody today saw the world long ago. So how do we learn about it? A historian is a person who studies the past. Historians look at sources. A source tells us something about the past. It can be a letter, a photo or a tool. It can be a story that an older person tells. Each source is a clue. We use clues as evidence. Evidence helps us make a claim about the past.

read.sections.1.text.back: Different sources can answer different questions about the past. The receipt shows the goods sold by a shop and the price of each item, so the receipt tells us that the price of rice was 12 tokens. The painting shows what the market looked like, with stalls, baskets and a wheelbarrow/pushcart. However, the painter may not have painted some details. The diary tells what one young person saw and did on market day. The diary says that traders arrived by boat before sunrise, but one person alone cannot see everything. So, historians always ask two questions: What does this source tell me, and what can it not tell me?
read.sections.1.text.source: Different sources can answer different questions about the past. The receipt shows what one shop sold and the price of each item, so it tells us that rice cost 12 tokens. The drawing shows what the market looked like, with stalls, baskets and a cart. However, the artist may have left some details out. The diary describes what one young person saw and did on market day. It says that traders arrived by boat before sunrise, but one person cannot see everything. So a historian always asks two questions: What does this source tell me, and what can it not tell me?

read.sections.1.simpler.back: Each source answers different questions. The receipt shows prices. The price of rice is 12 tokens. The painting shows what the market looks like. But the painter may not have painted everything. The diary tells what one young person saw. The diary says traders came by boat. But one person alone cannot see everything. So, ask two questions. What does this source tell me? What does it not tell me?
read.sections.1.simpler.source: Each source answers different questions. The receipt shows prices. Rice cost 12 tokens. The drawing shows what the market looked like. But the artist may leave things out. The diary tells what one young person saw. It says traders came by boat. But one person cannot see everything. So ask two questions. What does this source tell me? What does it not tell me?

read.sections.2.text.back: One source almost never tells the complete story, so historians compare sources. Comparing means looking at two things and noticing their similarities or differences. The painting shows a river, and the diary says that traders came by boat. Together, these clues suggest that the river helped people carry goods to the market. Historians also ask who made each source, and why they made it. Some questions are still unanswered, because no source tells us how many people lived in Riverstone. A strong claim explains what the evidence shows and what we still do not know.
read.sections.2.text.source: One source almost never tells the whole story, so historians compare sources. To compare means to look at two things and notice how they are similar or different. The drawing shows a river, and the diary says that traders came by boat. Together, these clues suggest that the river helped people bring goods to the market. A historian also asks who made each source, and why they made it. Some questions stay open, because none of the sources tells us how many people lived in Riverstone. A strong claim explains what the evidence shows and what we still do not know.

read.sections.2.simpler.back: One source does not tell the complete story. So, historians compare sources. They look for what is the same and what is different. The painting shows a river. The diary talks about boats. So, the river may have helped traders get to the market. There are things we still do not know. No source mentions how many people lived there. A good claim states what we know. The claim also states what we do not know.
read.sections.2.simpler.source: One source does not tell the whole story. So historians compare sources. They look for what is the same and what is different. The drawing shows a river. The diary talks about boats. So the river may have helped traders get to the market. Some things we still do not know. No source says how many people lived there. A good claim says what we know. It also says what we do not know.

write.example.back: I think Riverstone Market used to be a busy place, a place where people bought and sold food. The painting shows stalls selling food and cloth. The painting also shows people carrying baskets. The diary also shows that the market was crowded. The diary says that traders came by boat before sunrise. Together, these sources suggest that the river helped traders carry goods to the market. But the sources do not tell us how many people lived in Riverstone. The sources also do not tell us what the market was like on other days.
write.example.source: I think Riverstone Market was a busy place where people traded food. The drawing shows stalls selling food and cloth. It also shows people carrying baskets. The diary also shows that the market was crowded. It says traders came by boat before sunrise. Together, these sources suggest that the river helped traders bring goods to the market. But the sources do not tell us how many people lived in Riverstone. They also do not tell us what the market was like on other days.

watch.summary.back: This short video explains primary sources. A primary source is made at the time you are studying, often by someone who was there. Letters, diaries, photos, receipts, maps and tools can be primary sources. The source does not have to be famous or special. An ordinary receipt can show the items people bought and their prices. A diary can show what someone saw and felt. But each primary source shows only part of the story. So, historians ask who made it, when and why. Then, they compare it with other sources. In this lesson, the painting, the receipt and the diary are all primary sources. Together, the sources tell us more than one source alone.
watch.summary.source: This short video explains primary sources. A primary source was made at the time you are studying, often by someone who was there. Letters, diaries, photos, receipts, maps and tools can all be primary sources. They do not have to be famous or special. An everyday receipt can show what people bought and what it cost. A diary can show what one person saw and felt. But each primary source shows only part of the story. So historians ask who made it, when, and why. Then they compare it with other sources. In this lesson, the drawing, the receipt and the diary are all primary sources. Together, they tell us more than any one of them alone.
